title: Sweet smell from car
h1: Why does my car smell sweet, like syrup?
metaDesc: Sweet, syrup-like smell from your car? It's usually leaking coolant. Answer a few questions to see where it's coming from and how urgent it is.
synonyms: sweet smell when heater is on
smells like antifreeze but no leak
intro: A sweet, syrup-like smell usually means engine coolant (antifreeze) is leaking somewhere. Where you smell it, and what the temperature gauge is doing, helps show how serious it may be. Answer the questions below to narrow down the likely source and the safest next step.
safety: If the temperature gauge is in the red, a temperature warning light is on, or steam is coming from under the hood, pull over safely and turn the engine off.
Never open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot. Hot coolant can spray out and burn you.
If the inside of the windshield fogs up so you can't see, pull over until it clears.
If thick white smoke pours from the exhaust, stop driving and turn the engine off.

q_gauge.q: Is the temperature gauge high or rising, is a temperature warning light on, or is there steam from under the hood?
q_gauge.help: The temperature gauge usually sits near the middle once the engine is warm. Some cars only have a warning light that turns red when the engine runs hot.

opts.a: Yes: the gauge is high or climbing, the warning light is on, or there's steam

q_where.q: Where do you notice the sweet smell most?

opts.a: Inside the car, especially with the heater or defroster on
Outside, near the front of the car or under the hood after driving
From the tailpipe, along with white exhaust smoke

q_inside.q: Do you notice any of these inside the car?

opts.a: A greasy film that fogs the inside of the windshield
Damp or wet carpet on the front passenger-side floor
The heater blows cold or only lukewarm air

q_puddle.q: After the car has been parked for a while, is there a puddle or drips under the front?
q_puddle.help: Slide a piece of light-colored cardboard under the engine overnight. Coolant is usually bright green, orange, pink or yellow and feels slightly slimy.

opts.a: Yes, a brightly colored, slightly slimy drip
Only clear water that drips after using the A/C
No puddle, but I smell it or see a wisp of steam after driving

q_smoke.q: How much white smoke comes from the tailpipe?
q_smoke.help: A little thin vapor on a cold morning that disappears once the engine warms up is normal condensation. Coolant smoke is thicker, smells sweet and keeps coming.

opts.a: Thick white smoke that keeps coming, even once the engine is warm
Light white smoke with a sweet smell, mostly at startup

result.title: The engine may be losing coolant and overheating
result.now: Pull over safely and switch the engine off. Keep the hood closed while steam or spray is escaping. Leave all coolant caps in place until the engine and radiator are fully cold. Arrange roadside help or a tow before restarting.
if: If the gauge only crept up a little and dropped back once you stopped, check the coolant level once the engine is cold. Still have it towed or checked where it sits rather than driving on.
If you see coolant pouring out or a burst hose, don't add coolant and restart. The engine will overheat again quickly.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: A sweet smell plus a high temperature reading usually means coolant is escaping and the engine can't shed its heat. Driving an overheating engine even a few more miles can warp or crack major parts, turning a hose or radiator repair into a much bigger engine repair.

causes.name: Burst or leaking coolant hose
causes.clues: Steam or spray from one spot under the hood, or a wet, sticky hose.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or water pump
causes.clues: Coolant dripping from the very front of the car or from the front of the engine.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke, or coolant disappearing with no visible leak.
causes.against: Less likely if you can see coolant spraying from a hose or the radiator.

shop: Combustion gas (block) test for a head gasket leak

result.title: Coolant may be leaking inside the engine and being burned
result.now: Park the car and don't run the engine. Have it towed to a shop or have a mobile mechanic diagnose it.
if: If the coolant tank is nearly empty, coolant is likely being lost fast. Running the engine risks overheating and serious damage.
If the oil on the dipstick looks milky or like chocolate milk, coolant may be mixing with the oil. Don't start the engine.
result.why: Thick, sweet-smelling white smoke usually means coolant is getting into the cylinders and burning off. A failed head gasket is the most common reason, but a cracked part or a leaking intake gasket can do the same, which is why a shop will usually run a block test and pressure test before deciding on a repair. Coolant in the oil can wreck the engine bearings.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: The engine overheated recently, coolant keeps dropping, or the engine runs rough at startup.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or engine block
causes.clues: A history of severe overheating, or freezing weather with weak coolant.
causes.against: Much less common than a head gasket leak.

causes.name: Leaking intake manifold gasket (some engines)
causes.clues: Coolant loss with milky oil but little or no overheating.

you: With the engine cold, check the coolant tank level.
Pull the oil dipstick and look for a milky, tan color.

result.title: A small amount of coolant may be getting into the engine
result.now: Read the coolant level through the reservoir only when the engine is fully cold. If it is between its marks, leave the level alone. Have the source of coolant loss checked. If the reservoir is empty, the gauge rises, or the oil looks milky, keep the engine off and arrange a tow.
if: If the smoke gets thicker or keeps coming once the engine is warm, stop driving and have it towed.
If the temperature gauge rises at all, a temperature warning light comes on, or the heater suddenly blows cold, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the check engine light flashes or the engine starts running rough, pull over and turn it off.
If the coolant level stays full for a week and the smoke stops, it may have been normal condensation. Still mention it at your next service.
result.why: Light, sweet-smelling smoke at startup can mean a small internal coolant leak that seeps in while the car sits. These leaks tend to grow, and catching one early can prevent overheating and bigger engine damage.

causes.name: Early head gasket leak
causes.clues: The coolant level slowly drops with no puddles, and the smoke is worst on the first start of the day.

causes.name: Leaking intake manifold gasket (some engines)
causes.clues: Slow coolant loss with no outside leak.

causes.name: Normal condensation
causes.clues: Cold or humid weather, and the vapor is thin and disappears within a few minutes.
causes.against: Condensation doesn't smell sweet and doesn't lower the coolant level.

you: Mark the coolant tank level with tape and check it again after a few days.
Check the oil dipstick for a milky color.
shop: Spark plug inspection for coolant contamination

result.title: The heater core may be leaking coolant into the cabin
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. If it's only a little low, top it up and book a repair within a few days. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the windshield fogs up so you can't see, pull over. Use the A/C with the defroster to clear it, and don't drive until you can see clearly.
If the temperature gauge starts to climb, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the heater suddenly blows cold or you see steam from the vents or under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
If kids or pets ride in the car, keep them away from the wet carpet. Coolant is poisonous.
result.why: The heater core is a small radiator behind the dashboard that heats the cabin with hot coolant. When it leaks, coolant vapor can come out of the vents, leaving a sweet smell and a greasy film on the glass, and liquid can soak the passenger-side carpet. A shop will usually pressure test the system to confirm it's the heater core and not a hose behind the engine.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: Greasy fog on the windshield, a sweet smell that's strongest with the heat on, or wet passenger-side carpet.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose or connection behind the engine
causes.clues: The smell is also strong under the hood near the back of the engine.

causes.name: Clogged A/C drain dripping water into the cabin
causes.clues: The wet carpet is clear water with no sweet smell or slimy feel.
causes.against: A sweet smell or greasy windshield points to coolant, not A/C water.

you: Look for damp carpet or film on the windshield without touching or smelling the liquid.
If the windshield is fogged or streaked enough to limit your view, park safely.
shop: Heater core and heater hose inspection

result.title: The coolant may be very low from a leak. Don't keep driving
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn off the engine. Once it's fully cold, check the coolant tank. Even if a top-up brings the heat back, have the leak found before relying on the car. If the tank is empty, have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If the temperature gauge is high, a temperature warning light is on, or you see steam, keep the engine off and let it cool before doing anything else.
If the gauge reads normal, don't rely on it. When coolant is very low, the sensor can read normal even though the engine is hot.
If you see white, sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust or the oil looks milky, don't restart the engine.
result.why: When the heater blows cold and you smell coolant, the level may have dropped so far that hot coolant isn't reaching the heater. The same low level can leave the engine close to overheating, even before the gauge shows it.

causes.name: External coolant leak (hose, radiator, water pump)
causes.clues: Drips or colored, crusty residue under the hood or on the ground.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: A greasy windshield film or wet passenger-side carpet.

causes.name: Internal leak such as a head gasket
causes.clues: No visible leak, and white, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Look for colored drips or crusty residue around hoses and the radiator.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test if no outside leak is found

result.title: Coolant appears to be leaking from the engine's cooling system
result.now: Read the coolant level through the reservoir only when the engine is fully cold. If it is between its marks, leave the level alone. Have the source of coolant loss checked. If the reservoir is empty, the gauge rises, or the oil looks milky, keep the engine off and arrange a tow.
if: If the drip is steady or forms a puddle bigger than your hand overnight, have it towed rather than driving it.
If the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the heater suddenly blows cold or you see steam from under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
Clean up the puddle. Coolant tastes sweet to pets and children and is poisonous.
result.why: A colorful, slimy drip under the front of the car is usually coolant. Small leaks often show up as a sweet smell when coolant drips onto hot engine parts. Leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant leads to overheating.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or radiator hose
causes.clues: The drip is near the very front of the car, or a hose looks wet or crusty.

causes.name: Failing water pump
causes.clues: Drips from the front of the engine, near the drive belts, or a crusty trail below the pump.

causes.name: Loose hose clamp or worn coolant tank cap
causes.clues: Small seepage at a hose end, or residue around the cap.

you: Put cardboard under the engine overnight to see where the drip lands.
Look for crusty white, green or orange residue on hoses and the radiator.

result.title: A small coolant seep may be burning off on hot engine parts
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold and top it up if it's a little low, then book a cooling system check when convenient. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it checked before driving.
if: If the coolant level drops noticeably in a week, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge ever climbs above normal, a temperature warning light comes on, or the heater suddenly blows cold, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see steam from under the hood or white, sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: A tiny leak may not drip to the ground at all. Instead, the coolant lands on the hot engine or exhaust and evaporates, which is why you smell it after driving. Clear water dripping after A/C use is usually normal condensation and isn't the source of the smell.

causes.name: Seeping hose connection or clamp
causes.clues: A damp or crusty spot where a hose connects.

causes.name: Small water pump or radiator seep
causes.clues: Dried, colored residue at the front of the engine or on the radiator.

causes.name: Coolant tank cap or overflow tank seep
causes.clues: Residue around the cap or a crack in the plastic tank.

you: Mark the coolant level with tape and recheck it after a few days of driving.
With the engine cold, look for dried, colored residue around hoses and the tank.
shop: Coolant leak dye test with UV light

result.title: A coolant leak is a likely cause. Check the level first
result.now: With the engine cold, check the coolant tank level. If it's a little low, top it up, watch the temperature gauge and have the leak found within a few days. If the tank is empty or well below MIN, have it inspected before driving.
if: If the temperature gauge rises, a temperature warning light comes on, the heater suddenly blows cold, or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see thick white, sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust, or the oil on the dipstick looks milky, don't drive. Have it inspected.
If the level is fine and stays steady for a week, the smell may be from something else, such as a spilled drink. Mention it at your next service anyway.
result.why: Engine coolant is the most common source of a sweet smell from a car. It can leak inside the engine, behind the dash or from the hoses and radiator. Checking the level is the quickest way to know whether coolant is actually going missing.

causes.name: External coolant leak
causes.clues: Colored drips under the front of the car.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: The smell is strongest inside with the heat on, or the windshield fogs with a greasy film.

causes.name: Something spilled inside the car
causes.clues: The coolant level stays full and the smell never changes with the heater or engine temperature.

you: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Look under the car for colored drips after it's been parked.
